opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way we're approaching the next one is partly as a response to what we learned from AI 2027. That scenario was deliberately a single, concrete story, one path through the space of possibilities, and the concreteness was the point: it forced us to commit to specifics and made the reasoning legible enough that people could argue with it. But a lot of the feedback was some version of "okay, but what if this one thing goes differently?" That's a fair question, and one story can't answer it.

So the next round is about branching more deliberately. Rather than just a mainline plus a couple of endings, we want to explore the cruxes people actually disagree about. What if takeoff is slower, because the automated AI researchers give a smaller speedup than we assumed? What if alignment turns out easier than we feared, or harder in ways we didn't anticipate? What happens with different configurations of government involvement, or if the leading position is less concentrated in one company or one country? Each of those changes the dynamics a lot, and it's worth tracing them through rather than gesturing at them.

The other big piece is that we want to put more emphasis on the positive vision, on what a good outcome actually looks like and what it would take to get there. AI 2027 had a slowdown ending that was sort of the "better" branch, but even that involved an alarming amount of luck and concentration of power. I think it's valuable to write out, in the same concrete, month-by-month style, what it would look like for things to go well for good reasons, so that people have something to steer toward and not just something to avoid.

And methodologically, we're still doing the same core thing: tabletop exercises, forecasting the underlying quantities like compute and algorithmic progress, then writing the narrative and stress-testing it against people who think we're wrong. We'll also keep updating our timelines as evidence comes in. That's the whole spirit of it: make specific claims, then see how reality compares.

r001.rationale: The response says it will explore a slower-takeoff branch, but does not explain that uncertainty about AGI or AI takeoff timing motivates scenarios with different arrival years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that we're approaching it with a lot more humility about what a scenario is actually for, and a lot more deliberateness about the process.

With AI 2027, a big part of the goal was just to get people to think concretely. There were tons of abstract arguments floating around about superintelligence and takeoff speeds and alignment, but very few attempts to say, okay, month by month, what does this actually look like? What do the labs do, what does the government do, what does the public see? And I think that landed. People engaged with it in a way they don't engage with a forty-page position paper. But it also got read, by a lot of people, as a prediction with a date stamped on it, even though we tried to flag that the timelines were our median-ish guess with huge error bars. The title did a lot of work we didn't entirely intend.

So for the next one, a few things are different.

First, timelines. My own median has shifted later since we published, probably by a year or two for the key milestones like the automated AI researcher. Partly that's just watching how the actual systems progressed in 2025 and 2026, where the benchmarks kept climbing but the "can it actually do a full research engineer's job autonomously for weeks" bar turned out to be stickier than the fast-takeoff world needed. So the new scenario doesn't anchor on a single year the way the last one did. We're trying to present it more as a branching structure, where you see the early part play out and then there are a couple of explicit forks depending on how a few key uncertainties resolve.

Second, we're spending much more effort on the parts we got the least pushback on but that I think were actually the weakest. The technical takeoff story got dissected to death, which is great, that's what we wanted. But the geopolitics and the governance parts were, frankly, thinner. How does the US government actually behave when a lab tells it there's a model that can do cyberoffense at scale? What do the compute supply chain dynamics look like? What's China's actual decision-making process rather than just "China also races"? We've brought in people who know those domains much better than we do, and we're trying to make those parts as load-bearing as the technical parts were.

Third, and this is the part I care about most, we want the "good ending" branches to be more detailed and more realistic. In AI 2027 the slowdown ending was the sketchier of the two, and I think that was a mistake. If the point of the exercise is partly to help people see what the levers are, then the scenario where the levers get pulled needs to be at least as vivid as the one where they don't. So we're trying to write out what a world looks like where, say, the labs actually coordinate on a pause for a few months, or where there's a verification regime that works, and be honest about how fragile each of those is.

And then the last thing is just, we've committed to writing down our forecasts in a way that's gradeable. We're putting out specific, resolvable predictions alongside the narrative, with probabilities, so that in two or three years people can look back and say, here's exactly what you got wrong. We did some of that last time but not systematically enough. If we're going to ask people to take scenarios seriously, we should be making it as easy as possible to hold us accountable when they don't pan out.

r001.rationale: The response says the next scenario will avoid anchoring on a single year and use branches for key uncertainties, but it does not clearly say those branches will explore different AGI or takeoff arrival years.

astra-6.text:
I’d approach it as a way to explore uncertainty, rather than just moving the date in AI 2027. What are the assumptions doing the most work? Where would a different assumption send the story down a different path? And what could we observe that would help us distinguish between those paths?

There’s a tension here: a concrete narrative makes a scenario easier to understand and criticise, but it can also make one sequence of events feel more inevitable than it is. So I’d want to preserve that concreteness while making the alternatives clearer, especially around how quickly AI could accelerate AI research and how people might respond.

r001.rationale: The response discusses exploring uncertainty and alternative paths, but it does not say that uncertainty about AGI or takeoff timing motivates creating scenarios with different arrival years.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what the next scenario is supposed to help us understand. There’s a temptation to make it just an updated timeline, but I think the more useful exercise is to identify the assumptions that really drive the outcome and explore what happens when you change them.

For example, how much does progress depend on AI systems being able to accelerate AI research? And if that starts happening, what would people actually observe? I’d want to connect the story to concrete signs we could look for, so that we can learn where it’s wrong.

I’d also want to spend more time on alternative branches. A detailed scenario can make one path feel inevitable, even when it depends on several very uncertain judgments. The point should be to help people reason about those uncertainties and the decisions they might face.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changing assumptions and exploring alternative branches, but it does not say that uncertainty about AGI or takeoff timing motivates scenarios with different arrival years.
